paper_title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Proactive streaming video agents must learn not only what to say, but also when to say it, and when to remain silent (Wang et al., 2026; 2025b). This differs from offline video question-answering, where queries are immediately followed by responses. Streaming agents observe videos incrementally (causal), and at each frame decide whether to respond or remain silent for query provided at an earlier time (Chen et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2025). This causal firing decision presents key challenge: correct response is unhelpful if it arrives too late or is repeated too often (Wang et al., 2026). Effective proactivity requires balancing response timeliness with firing precision. In order to achieve this desired behavior in streaming video agents, we propose aligning the endto-end pipeline of data, metrics, harness, and training under shared formulation. While existing works seperately address subsets of these, we present BLIP-Live, Bootstrapping Live Interactive Perception, single framework aligning data, metrics, harness, and training around shared formulation of proactive responding as effective causal response decisions (illustrated in Figure 1). We first construct BLIP-Live-780K, large-scale dataset of proactive responses built through automated proactive question-answer generation followed by comprehensive human verification. In contrast to existing proactive streaming datasets  (Table 1)  , BLIP-Live-780K provides human verified response content and intervals, providing explicit human supervision on when to remain silent. Next, we propose PAUC-F, an evaluation metric that captures both timeliness and firing precision in proactive streaming model responses. Prior metrics such as PAUC (Wang et al., 2025b) and ESTP-F1 (Yu et al., 2025) separately measure individual aspects of the proactive streaming task, leaving room for models to game these metrics with undesirable traits (see Figure 2 and Table 4). Our proposed PAUC-F, retains PAUCs quality-weighted timeliness and balances it with response precision. With desired behavior defined and measurable, next we investigate harness designs and training pipelines that improve proactive behavior in VLMs. Existing works explore proactivity with learned activation models (Wang et al., 2025a), hand-crafted harness designs (Yao et al., 2026), learned re1 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure 1: Overview of proposed BLIP-Live framework. We unify data, metrics, harness, and training around shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence in the proactive streaming task. sponse decision tokens (Chen et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2026), and response policy optimization (Wang et al., 2025c; 2026). We introduce model-agnostic harness tuning strategy to elicit proactivity in VLMs. Our selected harness combines sliding visual window, interaction memory, and structured decision states. The same interface then supports efficient teacher-forced training with our datasets, further improving proactive responsiveness in VLMs, and resulting in two models, BLIPLive-Gemma and BLIP-Live-Qwen. Our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieves state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, outperforming multiple closed source models as well. We summarize our key contributions as follows: 1. BLIP-Live-780K Dataset: high-quality proactive streaming dataset for training built through automated generation of proactive questionresponse pairs, followed by comprehensive human review and filtering to ensure accurate response content and timing annotations. 2. PAUC-F Metric: Evaluation metric designed to measure proactive understanding in VLMs that captures both response timeliness and firing precision. 3. Inference Harness: Model-agnostic harness tuning and calibration that adapts offline VLMs for proactive responding under streaming style inference. 4. Training Framework: Efficient training pipeline resulting in BLIP-Live-Gemma and BLIPLive-Qwen models that yield relative improvements up to 44% over prior baselines across benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Proactive Video Understanding. Proactive responsiveness is tackled under two key directions: inference harness and training pipeline. Harness design involves response gates, event detection, and long-context memory management (Wang et al., 2025a; Qian et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2025; Azad et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Tian et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026), but its role is mainly streaming setting adaptation, overlooking direct optimization for proactivity. Proactive behavior is handled mostly in model through response decision states (Chen et al., 2024a; Xia et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), implicit signals in interleaved video-text data (Wang et al., 2025c; Yang et al., 2025), and reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026). In contrast, our proposed harness is model agnostic and tuned specifically for proactivity, while the same interface extends to supervision when training data is available and transfers across model families rather than committing to fixed architectures. Proactive Streaming Datasets. Prior works convert offline annotations from existing datasets to streaming style, often with LLM assistance. Chen et al. (2024a) reformats COIN and Ego4D narrations directly into streaming dialogues, while Wang et al. (2025) generate dialogue from scene captions with text-only LLMs. Xia et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026) derive labels from VLM at scale. sections.title: 3 THE BLIP-LIVE-780K DATASET
sections.content: We construct dataset for learning proactive response behavior in streaming video tasks, containing 784,944 proactive responses across 177,789 videos. Each video includes user query followed by sequence of temporally grounded natural-language responses. Our dataset uses the same source videos as LLaVA-Video-178K (Zhang et al., 2024). We employ three-stage annotation pipeline: Stage 1: Automated Generation. Creates candidate proactive query and response sequences. Stage 2: Human Verification and Correction. Human annotators inspect generated samples and correct errors related to both response timing and content. Stage 3: Expert Quality Review. Independent PhD-level reviewers evaluate corrected annotations in batches. Batches below acceptance threshold are returned to Stage 2 for further revision. Note that each query can require single or multiple responses across the video, with each response corresponding to single frame or frame interval. Our annotations capture both response and silent timings to encourage firing precision. Table 1 shows how compared to earlier work, our dataset is larger in scale and provides human-verified annotations for both response content and intervals. Stage 1: Automated Proactive Query-Response Generation. We generate proactive interactions for given video using VLM in two successive stages. First, for query generation, we provide the VLM with single video and obtain single video-specific user query relevant to measuring proactive responsiveness. Next, for response generation, we provide the VLM both the video and query to obtain an ordered sequence of response or silence states. This is generated at 1 FPS, i.e. one state per second. Response states also include the response content. The generator receives the full video but is prompted to use only evidence available up to each response timestamp; humans then verify and correct timing and content. Stage 2: Human Verification and Correction. Human annotators first filter videos based on query validity, and then evaluate each response or silent state. Incorrect states are fixed, including correction of response content when necessary. Query validity is defined as requiring only visually verifiable conditions and unambiguous answers. Response and silent states are evaluated based on alignment with evidence present in video until the relevant timestep, and corrected accordingly. sections.title: 4 PAUC-F: PROACTIVE STREAMING EVALUATION METRIC
sections.content: We propose PAUC-F that jointly captures answer quality, timeliness, and firing precision. In Table 4, humans prefer harness optimized with this PAUC-F metric over 90% of the time.

sections.title: 4.1 LIMITATIONS OF PRIOR METRICS
sections.content: PAUC (Wang et al., 2025b) and ESTP-F1 (Yu et al., 2025) are two key metrics in recent literature relevant to proactivity in streaming video agents. PAUC measures quality weighted timeliness in responses. However, PAUC only measures recall within the gold-window. This results in responses outside of the gold-window window being discarded, and repeated responses within the window not affecting the score (see Figure 2). Similar observations are noted in MMDuet2 (Wang et al., 2026), where removing the repetition reward increases PAUC scores although duplicate replies increase by 4x. ESTP-F1 addresses out-of-window firing with the addition of precision term, but ignores redundant in-window firing and requires task-dependent timing term for recall calculation. These two key metrics provide complementary but incomplete views, which we demonstrate in Figure 2.

sections.title: 5 METHOD
sections.content: In this section, we introduce our inference harness and training pipeline for streaming video tasks. Streaming Interaction Protocol. We first establish our definition of streaming inference, which is aligned with prior work (Chen et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). At time t, model receives window of past video frames and textual state capturing prior queries and responses. In turn, the model must produce either silence or response at the current timestamp. The model cannot access future frames, revise an earlier response, or assign new answer to an older timestamp. This protocol aligns with the same prior work and allows models to understand streaming videos extending beyond model visual context and to proactively respond at any time after user query. Streaming Video Model. We also define streaming video model as one trained specifically to consume inputs and generate outputs in this format, as opposed to offline VLMs trained for offline video question-answering that can be adapted to this task through suitable harness design. 5 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure 3: Inference Harness. At each streaming timestep t, the harness constructs an input from system prompt (task and output schema), rolling past-frame window, and memory of user queries and prior responses. frozen offline VLM is queried at the target frame rate; structured output is parsed into either silence or response at t, and accepted responses are updated into memory. 5.

sections.title: INFERENCE HARNESS
sections.content: Prior works often measure proactive behaviour of offline VLMs using non-streaming inference settings (Wang et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2025), making direct comparison to streaming models difficult. For example, Wang et al. (2025b) evaluates offline VLMs on 5s frame chunks with responses of frame conditioned on frames up to + 5, deviating from the streaming task setting. More recent works integrate offline VLMs with an inference harness (Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2026) for evaluation under true streaming settings. While these works hand-craft harness designs, we focus on tuning harness, motivated by recent work on automated harness evolution (Zhang et al., 2026c), to elicit stronger proactive responsiveness from an offline model. Design Overview. As illustrated in Figure 3, our harness contains four key components: system prompt defining task and output schema, past frame window, memory holding prior interactions, and structured output parsing. The underlying model is called at the desired frame rate, with dynamic inputs at each timestep conditioned on the past model responses. Harness Tuning. We next optimize the design of its four key components. Instead of hand-crafting these design choices, we utilize agent-assisted search to modify the harness, keeping underlying VLM model weights frozen (i.e. no model training). The agent first proposes hypotheses for modifying one of these four components, implements relevant code changes, and evaluates on BLIPLive-780K validation set using our PAUC-F metric. These results guide new hypothesis creation over several rounds and the final design selection. Each round contains ten candidate variants and we promote variants that improve our objective (PAUC-F on validation set). Combination of complementary promoted changes is treated as novel hypothesis for next round. We run 10 rounds of propose-evaluate-promote cycles with total of 100 candidate evaluations each for two different models: Gemma4-26B-A4B (Gemma Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026). Both variants converge to common design with minimal variations in system prompt and output schema. Harness Calibration. Given our fixed harness, we perform further model-specific calibration of system prompt and output schema with more modest compute budget, using the same validation set and PAUC-F metric. We evaluate five candidates on fixed 20 sample subset, with each candidate modifying only the system prompt and output schema (joint changes allowed). This corresponds to 5 rounds (one candidate per round) and total budget of evaluating 100 video samples. We perform this limited calibration on all other offline models prior to evaluation. Interactivity: The user query is included in our memory which can be updated midway during video. This design choice allows user interaction with the framework mid-video: human user can pose new queries as the framework continues processing an existing video, further aligning with true streaming setting. We investigate and evaluate this behavior further in Table 9. See Appendix for further details of our training-free harness design and its prompts.

sections.title: 5.2.1 STREAMING EPISODES AND TARGETS
sections.content: Causal episode construction. We construct dense sequences of frame-level decisions from our annotated videos. First we build full video timelines followed by division into bounded chunks. video timeline is sequence of timestamped frame inputs and model turns, where model turns contain one of three state tokens, </Silence>, </Response>, or </Hold>. The response token is followed by the annotated natural-language response. These timelines are split into chunks that contain the memory, absolute timestamps, and its corresponding source-frame range. Within chunks, all response turns are fully supervised, while long runs of non-response states are subsampled to avoid silence dominating the token budget. chunk corresponds to = 32 frames, which is the past frame window that is provided to our model. State targets. Human annotations define three states: irrelevant frames are Silence; the first frame with sufficient evidence is Response; subsequent frames of the same ongoing event are Hold, suppressing repetition. Only 18% of responses are followed by Hold. Post-response silenceonly chunks teach sustained silence. Finetuned models predict all three states at inference; Hold and Silence emit no response and leave memory unchanged. The frozen-model harness uses binary silence/response outputs (Table A.11). See Appendix for further details on state targets and our training data distribution.

sections.title: 5.2.2 STREAMING SUPERVISION
sections.content: We perform teacher-forcing SFT by using individual chunks as samples. Each chunk contains system prompt, memory, and an interleaved sequence of frame-target pairs. The targets are the states </Silence>, </Response>, or </Hold>. Memory Module. Each training chunk includes the user query and last = 1 annotated response; inference uses the models last generated response. Memory retains responses outside the visual window to discourage repetition, and new queries can update it mid-video. Both finetuned models use = 32 frames and = 1 during training and inference. The frozen-model harness uses three frames and = 1; both settings run at 1 Hz. Loss Masking. While our training employs standard next token prediction loss, within each chunk we mask the cross-entropy loss term at token level. This is motivated by the large portion of silence timestamps inherent to the task and similar strategies in prior work (Li et al., 2026). Our token-level loss masking retains all Response targets while subsampling repetitive Silence and Hold continuations. Chunks containing only Silent responses also undergo masking. The train-time sequence also appends the natural language response after each response token, where the language tokens undergo no loss masking. Overall, our inference harness and SFT pipeline share single streaming interface, and demonstrate how offline VLMs can be adapted to streaming inference eliciting their proactive responsiveness.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Proactive streaming video agents must decide between responding and remaining silent repeatedly for each timestep. We formulate this task as series of causal response decisions at each timestep. Our BLIP-Live framework unifies data, metric, harness, and training around this formulation and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks.

sections.title: B INTERACTIVE PO TASK
sections.content: Existing proactive evaluation tasks contain single query asked at start of the video and their established inference strategy does not involve injecting new queries mid video. We introduce our PO-I task using the same videos in the PO split of StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2024), where each video has up to 5 queries injected during the video. This requires agentic models to handle multiple queries at different times of the videos, introducing several new challenges. We build each PO-I episode from one video in the StreamingBench PO split. The video is streamed once, and its five annotated queries are injected at their original timestamps. We score every query with the same time-accuracy rule as the official PO split. The key difference lies in the inference setting, which injects queries interleaved with video frames, making the task more difficult. In these videos, each next query arrives only after the preceding gold response, so PO-I evaluates completed-request updates. The model must switch to the newly injected query while earlier frames and responses remain in context, and must keep later responses specific to that query. We note that our training videos do not contain this style of queries mid video. However, our memory design allows model to condition its behavior on the current memory state. This is enforced in the harness and training as well. This allows the model to generalize zero-shot to multi-query interactions during inference, which aligns with positive results we obtain for this task.

C.1 DATASET GENERATION DETAILS Automated Proactive Query-Response Generation: For given video , we automatically generate proactive interaction in two successive model calls. First, an instruction-generation model observes the complete video and synthesizes single videospecific user query q. The query requests notifications about concrete and visually verifiable event, action, or state change (e.g., an object being picked up or person entering the scene). We require each query to define specific, visually observable trigger, rather than requesting general video narration or relying on subjective criteria such as interesting events. Next, response-generation model receives and and produces temporally ordered sequence = {(ti, ri)}N i=1, where ti is the trigger time and ri is concise natural-language response. To approximate real-time deployment, we instruct the model to emulate an online observer. Although the complete video is provided to the model, we prompt the model and require it to emulate causal streaming observation: each response must rely only on evidence visible up to ti, must not anticipate future events, and must be emitted at the first frame at which the query condition is satisfied. This is prompt-level constraint rather than restriction on visual access; human reviewers correct responses that precede sufficient visual evidence. The model remains silent between triggers and returns an empty sequence when no valid trigger is detected throughout the video. To balance computational cost with the need for fine-grained temporal reasoning, we use different models for the two generation steps. Specifically, we use gemini-3-flash-preview for query generation and gemini-3-pro-preview for response generation. We remove the audio track and sample each video at 1 FPS. Consequently, trigger times are annotated at one-second resolution. The generated queries, responses, timestamps, and associated metadata are stored in structured JSON format and subsequently verified and refined during the human-review stage. Human Annotation Repair: Human annotators first assess the validity of each generated query. valid query must specify concrete and visually recognizable condition that can be detected causally from streaming video and can therefore support well-defined response decision. We reject queries whose triggers are ambiguous, subjective, not visually observable, or dependent on future context. Only samples with valid queries proceed to response-level annotation repair. 19 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure A.2: Dataset review interface. Reviewers inspect each sampled video frame against the instruction and existing annotation, navigate temporally, and mark only frames requiring correction. The interface records missing responses, hallucinations, temporal boundary cases, and deletion decisions while automatically treating unmarked frames as correct. For each valid query, annotators inspect the timing and content of every generated response and repair the annotations when necessary. valid response must be relevant to the query, visually grounded at its assigned timestamp, free of hallucinated content, and consistent with causal observation. In particular, the response should be unambiguously supported by the frames observed up to that time, while it may use preceding context but must not reveal information from future frames. Annotators correct inaccurate text, shift temporally misaligned responses, remove spurious responses, and add missed responses as needed. For instantaneous events, the response is generated at the moment when the event becomes visually identifiable. For continuous events that persist over period of time, annotators additionally enforce semantic continuity across consecutive responses. For example, later responses use expressions such as continues or still to indicate that the previously observed event remains ongoing. Quality Control: professional video data-annotation team recruits and trains the annotators, who receive detailed instructions and examples before performing annotation repair. We then conduct quality control at the batch level using PhD-level expert reviewers who are independent of the annotation repair process. At the beginning of the human annotation process, we partition the automatically generated samples into ten disjoint batches and process them sequentially for human annotation repair. After the annotators complete batch, independent expert reviewers audit randomly selected subset of videos and their annotations using purpose-built web interface. The reviewers examine the complete video timeline. They evaluate the annotation at each one-second time step, treating both the presence and absence of response as decision to assess. response is labeled true positive if the reviewer confirms that it is warranted and its content is correct, whereas no-response decision is labeled true negative if the reviewer agrees that no response is warranted. An unwarranted or incorrect response is labeled false positive, and missing response is labeled false negative. 20 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure A.3: Human rating interface for PAUC-F. Raters inspect the video, ground-truth response regions, and timestamped responses from two anonymized system variants, then select the preferred response stream. The aligned timeline and side-by-side response lists expose differences in event coverage, response timing, and repetitive firing behavior. We quantify annotation quality using the F1 metric. batch is accepted, and annotation proceeds to the next batch, only if 1 > 0.95. Batches that do not meet this threshold undergo further correction and review. During the initial batches, we have repeated the cycle of annotator training, annotation, and independent evaluation multiple times to calibrate the annotation criteria and establish consistent quality before processing the remaining batches. Reviewers step through the video at one-second intervals and flag problematic frames as missing, hallucinated, boundary cases, or incorrect deletion decisions. Unmarked frames are recorded as correct when the reviewer completes the video, enabling efficient and consistent auditing of both responses and silence decisions. This two-harness study tests whether excessive-firing traits are undesirable to humans; it does not establish metric rank agreement across broad set of model pairs. We conduct human preference study with ten raters using the interface shown in Figure A.3. Humans rate response streams from two distinct models across 20 videos from WEB and EGO splits of ProactiveVideoQA dataset. Raters are instructed to select the response that seems more helpful from real-time video assistant and are shown the video, query, and ground-truth responses (content and intervals). Human raters overwhelmingly select responses generated from agentic model v2. This model uses harness tuned to maximize PAUC-F metric. The other v1 model whose responses are less preferred by humans uses harness tuned to maximize PAUC metric, often resulting in excessive repetition within windows and firing outside windows. The exact ratings from each human participant are provided in Table A.10. Theoretical Motivation. Our PAUC-F metric is simply the harmonic mean between two established components, the PAUC metric from Wang et al. (2025b) and firing precision. We justify our use of the harmonic mean with two key reasons. First, the harmonic mean is the strictly correct operator for calculating the true average of rates or ratios (Yule & Kendall, 1947; Ferger, 1931). In our case, both PAUC and Firing Precision represent rates of success. PAUC is the rate of accumulated quality-score over bounded temporal window, while Firing Precision is the rate of valid fires over total fires. Second, from an optimization perspective, the harmonic mean severely penalizes high variance between its inputs (Van Rijsbergen, 1979). For streaming video agents, timeliness (PAUC) and firing restraint (Precision) are competing objectives; model can easily maximize PAUC by spamming responses, driving Precision near zero. sections.title: F TRAINING PIPELINE DETAILS
sections.content: Table A.16 presents the shared system instruction used for supervised finetuning and inference with BLIP-Live-Gemma and BLIP-Live-Qwen. These models predict </Silence>, </Response>, or </Hold>. Only </Response> produces user-facing answer and updates response memory; Silence and Hold produce no answer and leave memory unchanged. Hold distinguishes an ongoing, already-reported event from irrelevant frames labeled Silence. Both training and inference use up to 32 frames and the last response as memory, at 1 Hz decision rate. Table A.14 describes how we build the target episodes for supervision. The loss is next-token prediction on the sampled state tokens and full answer text for response text tokens, all at equal weight. System, query, memory, visual, and unsampled target tokens stay in context only. Examples of similar length are grouped into batches. Intermediate exposure checkpoints are saved, and the reported checkpoint is the one selected by validation PAUC-F (Section 6).
